q: Rate-limiting step of Heme synthesis?
a: δ-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) synthase (requires Vitamin B6).

q: Location of the erythropoietin (EPO) sensor in the kidney?
a: Peritubular interstitial cells of the renal cortex.

q: What state must iron be in to bind Oxygen?
a: Ferrous state (Fe<sup>2+</sup>). ("It 2nd-ly binds O<sub>2</sub>").

q: Major hemoglobin type in adults (HbA1) composition?
a: α<sub>2</sub>β<sub>2</sub>.

q: Major hemoglobin type in fetuses (HbF) composition?
a: α<sub>2</sub>γ<sub>2</sub>.

q: Why does HbF have higher oxygen affinity than HbA?
a: Decreased binding of 2,3-BPG to the γ-subunits.

q: Define "Reticulocyte Index" (RI) indicating adequate marrow response to anemia.
a: RI > 2%.

q: Most common cause of Iron Deficiency Anemia in elderly males?
a: GI blood loss (occult malignancy until proven otherwise).

q: Lab findings in Iron Deficiency Anemia (Ferritin, TIBC, Serum Fe)?
a: ↓ Ferritin, ↑ TIBC, ↓ Serum Iron.

q: Classic triad of Plummer-Vinson Syndrome?
a: Iron deficiency anemia, Esophageal webs, Glossitis.

q: Primary defect in Sideroblastic Anemia?
a: Protoporphyrin synthesis defect (lead poisoning, Vitamin B6 deficiency, X-linked ALA synthase defect).

q: Classic biopsy finding in Sideroblastic Anemia (Prussian Blue stain)?
a: Ringed sideroblasts (iron-laden mitochondria surrounding the nucleus).

q: Genetic defect in α-Thalassemia?
a: Gene deletion (Chromosome 16).

q: Genetic defect in β-Thalassemia?
a: Point mutation in splice sites/promoter sequences (Chromosome 11).

q: Hemoglobin electrophoresis finding in β-Thalassemia Minor?
a: ↑ HbA2 (> 3.5%).

q: Skull X-ray finding in β-Thalassemia Major?
a: "Crew-cut" appearance (marrow expansion).

q: Basophilic stippling is most associated with which Microcytic Anemia?
a: Lead Poisoning (inhibition of pyrimidine 5'-nucleotidase).

q: Distinguishing lab finding between B12 and Folate deficiency?
a: Methylmalonic acid (MMA) is elevated in B12 deficiency ONLY.

q: Neurological symptom associated with B12 deficiency?
a: Subacute Combined Degeneration (SCD) of the spinal cord (dorsal columns/lateral corticospinal tract).

q: Most common cause of Vitamin B12 deficiency?
a: Pernicious Anemia (anti-intrinsic factor antibodies).

q: Type of cell seen on peripheral smear in Megaloblastic Anemia?
a: Hypersegmented neutrophils (> 5 lobes).

q: Common drug causes of Folate deficiency?
a: Phenytoin, Methotrexate, Trimethoprim.

q: Two major categories of Normocytic Anemia based on Reticulocyte Count?
a: Hemolytic (High RC) vs. Non-hemolytic/Underproduction (Low RC).

q: Intravascular Hemolysis: Serum Haptoglobin levels?
a: Decreased (Haptoglobin binds free Hemoglobin).

q: Confirmatory test for Hereditary Spherocytosis?
a: Osmotic Fragility Test (or Eosin-5-maleimide flow cytometry).

q: Mechanism of Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria (PNH)?
a: Acquired PIGA gene mutation → deficiency of GPI anchor → loss of CD55/CD59 (complement inhibitors).

q: Triad of PNH?
a: Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia, Pancytopenia, Venous thrombosis (e.g., Budd-Chiari).

q: Amino acid substitution in Sickle Cell Anemia (HbS)?
a: Glutamic acid to Valine at position 6 of β-globin chain.

q: Amino acid substitution in Hemoglobin C (HbC)?
a: Glutamic acid to Lysine at position 6 of β-globin chain. ("LyCine").

q: Most common trigger for G6PD deficiency oxidative stress?
a: Fava beans, Infections, Sulfa drugs, Primaquine.

q: Histologic hallmark of G6PD deficiency?
a: Heinz bodies and Bite cells.

q: Warm Agglutinin AIHA: Antibody type and association?
a: IgG; associated with SLE and CLL.

q: Cold Agglutinin AIHA: Antibody type and association?
a: IgM; associated with Mycoplasma pneumoniae and Mononucleosis.

q: Translocation associated with Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML)?
a: t(9;22); BCR-ABL (Philadelphia chromosome).

q: Marker used to differentiate CML from a Leukemoid Reaction?
a: Leukocyte Alkaline Phosphatase (LAP). Low in CML, High in Leukemoid Reaction.

q: Classic marker for Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML)?
a: Auer Rods (MPO positive).

q: Specific treatment for AML M3 (Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia)?
a: All-trans Retinoic Acid (ATRA).

q: Most common childhood leukemia?
a: Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL).

q: Translocation associated with Burkitt Lymphoma?
a: t(8;14); c-myc activation.

q: Translocation associated with Follicular Lymphoma?
a: t(14;18); BCL-2 activation.

q: Translocation associated with Mantle Cell Lymphoma?
a: t(11;14); Cyclin D1 activation.

q: Diagnostic cell for Hodgkin Lymphoma?
a: Reed-Sternberg cell ("Owl's eye" appearance; CD15+, CD30+).

q: Clinical hallmark of Multiple Myeloma?
a: CRAB: Hypercalcemia, Renal insufficiency, Anemia, Bone lytic lesions.

q: Pathognomonic urine finding in Multiple Myeloma?
a: Bence-Jones protein (Ig light chains).

q: Role of von Willebrand Factor (vWF) in primary hemostasis?
a: Adhesion of platelets to subendothelial collagen via GpIb receptor.

q: Platelet receptor for Fibrinogen (aggregation)?
a: GpIIb/IIIa.

q: Coagulation factor deficiency in Hemophilia A?
a: Factor VIII.

q: Coagulation factor deficiency in Hemophilia B?
a: Factor IX.

q: Lab profile of DIC (Platelets, PT/PTT, Fibrinogen, D-dimer)?
a: ↓ Platelets, ↑ PT/PTT, ↓ Fibrinogen, ↑ D-dimer.

q: Deficiency in Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP)?
a: ADAMTS13 (vWF cleaving protease).

q: Pentad of TTP?
a: Fever, Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA), Thrombocytopenia, Renal failure, Neurological symptoms.

q: Effect of Aspirin on platelet function?
a: Irreversible inhibition of COX-1 (inhibits TXA<sub>2</sub> synthesis).

q: Mechanism of Heparin?
a: Activates Antithrombin III.

q: Antidote for Heparin overdose?
a: Protamine sulfate.

q: Mechanism of Warfarin?
a: Inhibits Epoxide Reductase (interferes with Vitamin K recycling).

q: Most common inherited hypercoagulable state?
a: Factor V Leiden (resistance to Protein C cleavage).

q: Mutation associated with Polycythemia Vera?
a: JAK2 kinase mutation.

q: Clinical symptom unique to Polycythemia Vera?
a: Aquagenic pruritus (itching after a hot bath).

q: Major complication of Essential Thrombocythemia?
a: Bleeding AND thrombosis (paradoxical).

q: Bone marrow finding in Myelofibrosis?
a: "Dry tap" (extensive fibrosis) and Teardrop RBCs (Dacrocytes).

q: Storage form of iron in the marrow?
a: Hemosiderin.

q: Target cells are typically seen in which three conditions?
a: HbC disease, Asplenia, Liver disease, Thalassemia. ("HALT").

q: Heinz bodies vs Howell-Jolly bodies (Composition)?
a: Heinz = Denatured Hemoglobin; Howell-Jolly = DNA remnants.

q: Sideroblastic Anemia vs Lead Poisoning (Enzyme inhibited)?
a: Sideroblastic = ALA Synthase; Lead = ALA Dehydratase & Ferrochelatase.

q: Primary site of heme degradation?
a: Splenic Macrophages (Heme → Biliverdin → Unconjugated Bilirubin).

q: Effect of CO<sub>2</sub> and H^+ (acid) on the Oxygen-Hemoglobin dissociation curve?
a: Right shift (Bohr effect) → increased O<sub>2</sub> unloading to tissues.

q: Schistocytes + Normal PT/PTT?
a: TTP or HUS.

q: Schistocytes + Prolonged PT/PTT?
a: DIC.

q: Isolated ↑ PTT that corrects with mixing study?
a: Factor deficiency (e.g., Hemophilia A/B).

q: Isolated ↑ PTT that does NOT correct with mixing study?
a: Coagulation factor inhibitor (e.g., Lupus Anticoagulant).

q: Massive Splenomegaly + Pancytopenia + TRAP positive?
a: Hairy Cell Leukemia.

q: Smudge cells on peripheral smear?
a: Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL).

q: Lytic bone lesions + Hypercalcemia + Rash?
a: Adult T-cell Leukemia/Lymphoma (HTLV-1).

q: "Starry sky" appearance on lymph node biopsy?
a: Burkitt Lymphoma.

q: Birbeck granules (tennis rackets) on EM?
a: Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis.

q: Eosinophilic inclusions in the cytoplasm of plasma cells in Multiple Myeloma?
a: Russell bodies.

q: Direct effect of 2,3-BPG on the hemoglobin oxygen affinity?
a: It stabilizes the T (Taut) state, shifting the curve to the right and promoting O<sub>2</sub> unloading.

q: Why is the ESR (Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate) increased in inflammation?
a: Fibrinogen (an acute phase reactant) coats RBCs, neutralizing their negative surface charge (Zeta potential) and allowing them to aggregate (Rouleaux).

q: Distinction between Hemoglobinuria and Myoglobinuria on dipstick?
a: Both show "Blood" on dipstick, but only Hemoglobinuria shows pink/red serum (Myoglobin is cleared rapidly, leaving serum clear).

q: What is the "Rule of Three" in RBC indices?
a: RBC × 3 ≈ Hb and Hb × 3 ≈ Hct.

q: Most common cause of Death in Sickle Cell patients (Adults)?
a: Acute Chest Syndrome.

q: Organism responsible for Osteomyelitis in Sickle Cell patients?
a: Salmonella (most common/classic) and Staphylococcus aureus.

q: Effect of Hydroxyurea in Sickle Cell Disease?
a: Increases production of HbF, which interferes with the polymerization of HbS.

q: Clinical finding in Lead Poisoning involving the gums?
a: Burton lines (bluish-gray lead sulfide deposits).

q: Mechanism of Bernard-Soulier Syndrome?
a: Deficiency of GpIb; impaired platelet-to-vWF adhesion.

q: Classic finding on peripheral smear for Bernard-Soulier?
a: Giant platelets (often as large as RBCs).

q: Mechanism of Glanzmann Thrombasthenia?
a: Deficiency/defect of GpIIb/IIIa; impaired platelet-to-platelet aggregation.

q: Ristocetin cofactor assay result in von Willebrand Disease (vWD)?
a: Abnormal (no agglutination), because vWF is required for Ristocetin-induced platelet clumping.

q: Why is the PTT sometimes prolonged in vWD?
a: vWF acts as a stabilizer/carrier for Factor VIII.

q: What is the "Pseudo-Thrombocytopenia" artifact in lab reports?
a: Platelet clumping in the test tube caused by EDTA (requires re-testing with a citrate tube).

q: Mechanism of Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura (ITP)?
a: Anti-GpIIb/IIIa antibodies → splenic macrophage consumption of platelets.

q: First-line treatment for ITP in a patient with a dangerously low platelet count?
a: IVIG (acts as a "decoy" for splenic macrophages) or Corticosteroids.

q: Effect of Protein C/S deficiency on the body?
a: Hypercoagulability; unable to inactivate Factors Va and VIIIa.

q: Why does Warfarin cause "Skin Necrosis" in Protein C deficient patients?
a: Protein C has a shorter half-life than Factors II, IX, and X; its rapid depletion creates a transient hypercoagulable state.

q: Mechanism of Antithrombin III deficiency?
a: PTT fails to rise significantly after giving Heparin (Heparin resistance).

q: Difference between UFH (Unfractionated Heparin) and LMWH (Enoxaparin) mechanism?
a: UFH inhibits both Thrombin and Factor Xa; LMWH predominantly inhibits Factor Xa.

q: Lab test used to monitor Warfarin therapy?
a: PT / INR.

q: Direct Thrombin Inhibitors (e.g., Argatroban, Bivalirudin) are the treatment of choice for?
a: Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT).

q: Mutation found in almost 100% of Hairy Cell Leukemia cases?
a: BRAF V600E.

q: Distinctive "Dry Tap" on bone marrow aspiration is seen in which two conditions?
a: Primary Myelofibrosis and Hairy Cell Leukemia.

q: Difference between Leukemoid Reaction and CML regarding Basophils?
a: Basophilia is characteristic of CML, not a Leukemoid Reaction.

q: Typical immunophenotype of CLL B-cells?
a: CD5+ and CD23+ (Note: CD5 is usually a T-cell marker).

q: What is a "Richter Transformation"?
a: CLL/SLL transforming into an aggressive Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma (DLBCL).

q: "Waldenström Macroglobulinemia" involves the overproduction of which Ig?
a: IgM (leads to hyperviscosity syndrome).

q: Radiographic "Punch-out" lesions in Multiple Myeloma are caused by?
a: RANKL activation of Osteoclasts (and inhibition of Osteoblasts).

q: Key difference between MGUS and Multiple Myeloma?
a: MGUS has < 10% plasma cells in marrow and NO "CRAB" symptoms.

q: Most common transfusion reaction?
a: Febrile Non-hemolytic Transfusion Reaction (caused by cytokines in stored blood).

q: Primary symptom of TRALI (Transfusion-Related Acute Lung Injury)?
a: Non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema (sudden onset respiratory distress/hypoxia).

q: Mechanism of Acute Hemolytic Transfusion Reaction?
a: Type II Hypersensitivity (preformed antibodies against donor ABO antigens).

q: Blood product used to rapidly reverse Warfarin?
a: Prothrombin Complex Concentrate (PCC) or Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP).

q: Indication for giving "Washed" Red Blood Cells?
a: IgA deficiency (to prevent anaphylaxis).

q: Storage lesion of RBCs involves a decrease in which metabolite?
a: 2,3-BPG (leads to increased O<sub>2</sub> affinity and decreased tissue delivery).

q: Definition of Pancytopenia?
a: Decrease in all three cell lines (RBCs, WBCs, and Platelets).

q: Most common cause of Aplastic Anemia?
a: Idiopathic (immune-mediated T-cell destruction of stem cells).

q: Morphology of RBCs in Myelophthisic Anemia?
a: Teardrop cells (Dacrocytes) – caused by the marrow being "squeezed" by fibrosis or tumor.

q: Deficiency in Acute Intermittent Porphyria (AIP)?
a: Porphobilinogen (PBG) deaminase.

q: The "5 Ps" of Acute Intermittent Porphyria symptoms?
a: Painful abdomen, Port wine-colored urine, Polyneuropathy, Psychological disturbances, Precipitated by drugs (CYP450 inducers).

q: Deficiency in Porphyria Cutanea Tarda (PCT)?
a: Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase.

q: Classic clinical presentation of Porphyria Cutanea Tarda?
a: Blistering cutaneous photosensitivity and hyperpigmentation (often associated with Hepatitis C).

q: Iron overload in the heart (Hemochromatosis) typically leads to?
a: Restrictive or Dilated Cardiomyopathy.

q: Marker for identifying Hematopoietic Stem Cells (HSC)?
Markers used to identify B-cell lineage via Flow Cytometry?
a: CD19, CD20, and CD21.

q: Marker used to identify the monocyte lineage?
a: CD14 (the receptor for LPS).

q: What does a "Shift to the Left" signify in a CBC?
a: Increased presence of immature neutrophils (band cells), usually indicating acute infection or inflammation.

q: How is the "Mentzer Index" used to differentiate Iron Deficiency from Thalassemia?
a: MCV / RBC count. If < 13, it suggests Thalassemia; if > 13, it suggests Iron Deficiency.

q: Meaning of "Anisocytosis" on a lab report?
a: Variation in RBC size (measured by RDW - Red Cell Distribution Width).

q: Meaning of "Poikilocytosis"?
a: Variation in RBC shape.

q: Mechanism of Parvovirus B19 induced anemia?
a: Directly infects and lyses Erythroid Precursor cells; causes Aplastic Crisis in patients with high RBC turnover (e.g., Sickle Cell).

q: Hallmark peripheral smear finding in Microangiopathic Hemolytic Anemia (MAHA)?
a: Schistocytes (Helmet cells).

q: What causes the "Starry Sky" appearance in Burkitt Lymphoma histology?
a: Tingible body macrophages (white "stars") consuming apoptotic B-cells (dark "sky").

q: Which enzyme is deficient in Methemoglobinemia?
a: Cytochrome b<sub>5</sub> reductase (Methemoglobin reductase).

q: Treatment for symptomatic Methemoglobinemia?
a: Methylene blue (reduces Fe<sup>3+</sup> back to Fe<sup>2+</sup>).

q: Clinical "classic" presentation of Methemoglobinemia?
a: Cyanosis (chocolate-colored blood) that does not improve with supplemental Oxygen.

q: Diagnostic hallmark of Myelodysplastic Syndromes (MDS)?
a: "Ringed Sideroblasts" and "Pseudo-Pelger-Huët anomaly" (bilobed neutrophils).

q: Major risk of Myelodysplastic Syndrome (MDS)?
a: Transformation into Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML).

q: In Polycythemia Vera, what happens to Serum Erythropoietin (EPO) levels?
a: EPO is low (negative feedback from high RBC mass).

q: Difference between "Primary" and "Secondary" Polycythemia?
a: Primary (PV) has low EPO; Secondary (Altitude, Smoking, RCC) has high EPO.

q: Term for marrow being replaced by "non-hematopoietic" material (tumor, granuloma)?
a: Myelophthisis.

q: Most common cause of Hydrops Fetalis?
a: α-Thalassemia (4-gene deletion; Hb Barts / γ4).

q: Most common clinical presentation of Diamond-Blackfan Anemia?
a: Rapid-onset anemia in the 1st year of life, short stature, and craniofacial/thumb anomalies.

q: Genetic defect in Fanconi Anemia?
a: DNA cross-link repair defect; leads to marrow failure and increased risk of AML.

q: Typical physical findings in Fanconi Anemia?
a: Cafe-au-lait spots, short stature, and absent/hypoplastic thumbs.

q: HbH disease involves how many α-globin gene deletions?
a: 3 gene deletions (β<sub>4</sub> tetramers).

q: What is "Extramedullary Hematopoiesis"?
a: RBC production outside the marrow (Spleen/Liver), often seen in Thalassemia or Myelofibrosis.

q: Pathogenesis of "Bony Bossing" in Thalassemia?
a: Reactive marrow hyperplasia expanding the marrow space, leading to "Chipmunk facies."

q: Cause of "Pain Crisis" in Sickle Cell Disease?
a: Vaso-occlusion (infarction) in small vessels due to sickled RBCs.

q: Immediate treatment for Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT)?
a: Stop Heparin immediately and start a Direct Thrombin Inhibitor (e.g., Argatroban).

q: Lab marker for effective B12 replacement therapy?
a: Significant increase in Reticulocyte count within 3-5 days.

q: Most common cause of Vitamin K deficiency in newborns?
a: Lack of gut flora and poor placental transfer (prevented by Vitamin K injection at birth).

q: Marker for identifying "Blast" cells in Acute Leukemia?
a: CD34 (marker of immaturity).

q: Most common genetic mutation in Systemic Mastocytosis?
a: KIT D816V mutation.

q: Enzyme deficient in Congenital Erythropoietic Porphyria (Gunther Disease)?
a: Uroporphyrinogen III cosynthase.

q: Effect of Hemolysis on Serum LDH (Lactate Dehydrogenase) and 왜?
a: LDH is significantly increased; it is an enzyme abundant inside RBCs released upon rupture.

q: What is the "Ham Test" (Acidified Serum Test) historically used for?
a: Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria (PNH) – superseded by flow cytometry for CD55/59.

q: "Pencil Cells" on peripheral smear are characteristic of?
a: Iron Deficiency Anemia.

q: "Acanthocytes" (Spur Cells) are most commonly associated with?
a: Liver disease or Abetalipoproteinemia.

q: "Echinocytes" (Burr Cells) are most commonly associated with?
a: Uremia (Renal Failure) or Pyruvate Kinase deficiency.

q: "Degmacytes" is the technical term for which cell type?
a: Bite Cells (seen in G6PD deficiency).

q: What are "Cabot Rings" and when are they seen?
a: Remnants of the mitotic spindle; seen in Megaloblastic Anemia or Lead Poisoning.

q: Mechanism of Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia (Osler-Weber-Rendu)?
a: Autosomal dominant disorder of blood vessels leading to telangiectasias and AVMs.

q: Screening test for Factor XIII deficiency?
a: 5-Molar Urea Solubility Test (Standard PT/PTT will be normal).

q: Function of Protein S?
a: Acts as a cofactor for Protein C to inactivate Factors Va and VIIIa.

q: What is "Lupus Anticoagulant" paradox?
a: It prolongs PTT in vitro but causes a hypercoagulable state (thrombosis) in vivo.

q: Most common cause of "Acquired" Hemophilia?
a: Autoantibodies against Factor VIII (often postpartum or malignancy-associated).

q: What are "Pitting" and "Culling" in the spleen?
a: Pitting: Removing inclusions (Heinz bodies) without destroying the cell. Culling: Removing damaged RBCs entirely.

q: Immunological consequence of Splenectomy?
a: Decreased IgM and decreased complement activation, leading to susceptibility to encapsulated organisms.

q: The "Encapsulated Trio" to vaccinate against post-splenectomy?
a: S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae type b, and N. meningitidis.

q: Cause of "Gaucher Cells" (crinkled paper appearance) in the marrow?
a: Glucocerebrosidase deficiency.

q: Specific antidote for Dabigatran?
a: Idarucizumab.

q: Specific antidote for Factor Xa inhibitors (Rivaroxaban/Apixaban)?
a: Andexanet alfa.

q: Primary side effect of Desmopressin (DDAVP) when treating vWD?
a: Hyponatremia (due to its ADH-like effect).

q: What is "Leucovorin Rescue" used for?
a: To reduce the toxicity of high-dose Methotrexate by providing a source of reduced folate.

q: Formula for Mean Corpuscular Hemoglobin Concentration (MCHC)?
a: MCHC = (Hemoglobin / Hematocrit) × 100.

q: What condition is the ONLY one with an increased MCHC?
a: Hereditary Spherocytosis (due to membrane loss and cellular dehydration).

q: Corrected Reticulocyte Count formula?
a: Retics % × (Hct / 45).

q: How many days does it take for a Reticulocyte to mature in the peripheral blood?
a: Approximately 1 day.

q: Differentiate "Iron Deficiency" vs "Anemia of Chronic Disease" via TIBC?
a: Iron Def: TIBC is ↑. Chronic Disease: TIBC is ↓.

q: Differentiate "Leukemoid Reaction" vs "CML" via Cytogenetics?
a: CML will have t(9;22); Leukemoid reaction will be cytogenetically normal.

q: Differentiate "TTP" vs "HUS" in clinical presentation?
a: HUS typically presents with bloody diarrhea (EHEC) and predominant renal failure; TTP has more neurological symptoms.

q: Differentiate "Follicular Lymphoma" vs "Reactive Lymph Node Hyperplasia"?
a: Follicular Lymphoma: BCL-2 (+), lacks tingible body macrophages, monoclonal.

q: Differentiate "Multiple Myeloma" vs "Primary Amyloidosis" (AL)?
a: MM is a plasma cell malignancy; AL is a protein folding disorder (misfolded light chains) often secondary to a plasma cell dyscrasia.

q: Most common inherited cause of Sideroblastic Anemia?
a: X-linked deficiency of ALAS2 (erythroid-specific δ-aminolevulinic acid synthase).

q: Direct effect of Lead on the heme pathway enzymes?
a: Inhibits Ferrochelatase and ALA Dehydratase.

q: Which enzyme deficiency is protected against P. falciparum malaria?
a: G6PD deficiency and Pyruvate Kinase deficiency.

q: Mechanism of Pyruvate Kinase (PK) deficiency?
a: ↓ ATP → rigid RBCs → extravascular hemolysis in the splenic red pulp.

q: Distinctive finding on peripheral smear for Pyruvate Kinase deficiency?
a: Echinocytes (Burr cells) that are not related to uremia.

q: What is the "TRAP" stain?
a: Tartrate-Resistant Acid Phosphatase; used for Hairy Cell Leukemia.

q: Typical immunophenotype for Hairy Cell Leukemia?
a: CD11c, CD25, CD103.

q: The "Sezary Syndrome" triad?
a: Erythroderma, Lymphadenopathy, and circulating Sezary cells (cerebriform nuclei).

q: Distinction between Myelofibrosis and CML on marrow biopsy?
a: Myelofibrosis shows "collagen fibrosis" (Silver/Reticulin stain); CML is hypercellular with myeloid maturation.

q: What is "Aleukemic Leukemia"?
a: Leukemia where the abnormal cells are confined to the marrow; the peripheral WBC count is normal or low.

q: Why is the "Bleeding Time" usually normal in Hemophilia?
a: Bleeding time tests primary hemostasis (platelets); Hemophilia is a defect in secondary hemostasis (clotting factors).

q: Mechanism of Tranexamic Acid (TXA)?
a: Antifibrinolytic; inhibits Plasminogen activation to Plasmin.

q: What is "Glucanzmann Thrombasthenia" vs "Bernard-Soulier" on Ristocetin test?
a: Bernard-Soulier: No agglutination with Ristocetin. Glanzmann: Normal agglutination with Ristocetin (but fails with ADP/Collagen).

q: What is the "Russell Viper Venom Time" (dRVVT) used for?
a: To confirm the presence of Lupus Anticoagulant (Antiphospholipid Syndrome).

q: What is "Hemoglobin Barts"?
a: γ4 (four gamma chains); seen in 4-gene deletion α-Thalassemia (Hydrops Fetalis).

q: What is "Hemoglobin H"?
a: β4 (four beta chains); seen in 3-gene deletion α-Thalassemia.

q: Effect of "Acidosis" on the P50 of the Oxygen-Hb curve?
a: Increases the P50 (shifts curve to the right, meaning lower affinity).

q: What is the "P50"?
a: The partial pressure of oxygen at which hemoglobin is 50% saturated.

q: Which Hemoglobin variant is most "Polymerization-prone"?
a: Deoxygenated HbS.

q: Why is Cimetidine or Sulfa drugs dangerous for G6PD patients?
a: They induce oxidative stress, leading to Hemolysis.

q: Treatment of choice for "Iron Overload" (Hemochromatosis)?
a: Therapeutic phlebotomy (or Deferoxamine/Deferasirox chelation if phlebotomy is contraindicated).

q: Common side effect of EPO (Erythropoietin) therapy?
a: Hypertension and increased risk of thromboembolic events.

q: What is the "D-dimer" specifically measuring?
a: Fibrin degradation products that have been cross-linked by Factor XIII.

q: Association: Thymoma?
a: Pure Red Cell Aplasia (PRCA) or Myasthenia Gravis.

q: Association: "Doughnut-shaped" nuclei in neutrophils?
a: Pseudo-Pelger-Huet anomaly (Myelodysplastic Syndrome).

q: Association: "Hyper-segmented" neutrophils + Glossitis?
a: Megaloblastic Anemia (B12 or Folate).

q: Association: Pruritus after a hot shower?
a: Polycythemia Vera (Mast cell degranulation).
